channel.title: The Tomorrow Post
channel.description: A newspaper for the digital age. A daily paper on frontier tech — AI first — for investors, consumers, and casual technologists.

item.title: Golden State Won the WNBA Title in Its Second Year, in the First Game 7 in Finals History
item.description: The Golden State Valkyries beat the Atlanta Dream 68–63 on Saturday to win the WNBA championship in the franchise's second season. Gabby Williams scored 28 of her 30 points in the second half and was named Finals MVP.
item.content:encoded:
The Golden State Valkyries won the WNBA championship on Saturday night, beating the Atlanta Dream 68–63 in Game 7 of the Finals at Chase Center — in the franchise's second year of existence. The Valkyries are the fastest expansion team in a major North American league to win a title, and the first team in the WNBA's 30-year history to win a championship without a single All-WNBA selection on its roster that season.

The game turned on one half. Gabby Williams scored 2 points in the first half and 28 in the second — the most in any half of a postseason game in league history — finishing with 30 and the Finals MVP award, including 15 consecutive Golden State points across the third and fourth quarters. Golden State trailed 30–24 at halftime, in the first Game 7 in Finals history. Owner Joe Lacob had promised a title within the team's first five years when the franchise was announced; the parade is scheduled for Wednesday in San Francisco.

item.title: The Week Every Claim Gets a Date
item.description: Apple and Palantir report tonight. Americans vote tomorrow. On Wednesday, Qwen testing begins inside Apple Intelligence in China and Moonshot's full Kimi weights fall due. Next week Anthropic takes its prospectus on the road. After a month of filings, valuations and commitments stated as intentions, the next seven days convert several of them into dated, checkable facts.
item.content:encoded:
The Tomorrow Post's October was a month of statements about the future, most of them dated in someone else's interest: a bridge round targeted at a Friday, a roadshow penciled for a November week, weights promised by a Wednesday. November's first full week is when a run of those statements meet dates that other people control.

Tonight, Apple and Palantir report after the close — the first earnings since Friday's selloff took the Nasdaq down 2.86% to its lowest close since July. Apple's consensus sits near $113 billion in revenue, and the report is its first under chief executive John Ternus, with memory costs climbing into the December-quarter guide. Palantir reports against a guide of $2.160 to $2.164 billion that consensus has already stepped over. One company tests whether consumer demand outruns a cost squeeze; the other tests whether enterprise AI spending shows up as revenue at the rate its valuation assumes.

Tomorrow, the test is electoral. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are decided, and the prediction markets covered in this edition settle a $1.4 billion claim to forecast the result. AMD reports the same evening. On Wednesday the tests turn technical: developers in China begin testing Qwen inside Apple Intelligence, and Moonshot's full Kimi K3.1 Pro weights fall due — a promise made on October 23, when the company also said it had removed cyber data from the open weights. Whether the released weights match the described model is checkable within days by anyone who downloads them.

None of these dates was set by the companies being tested, which is what distinguishes the week. A roadshow can slip and a round can be resized — October showed both. An election, an earnings calendar, a promised file and a regulator's deadline cannot be resized by their subjects. By Friday's jobs report, and certainly by Anthropic's roadshow in the week of November 9, several of the numbers this paper has carried as intentions will have become results, and the dossiers will record which ones survived contact with their dates.

item.title: Prediction Markets Have Traded More Than $1.4 Billion on the Midterms, One Day Before the Vote
item.description: Trading on 2026 midterm markets passed $1.4 billion in CNN's analysis — nearly $1.1 billion of it on Kalshi and more than $340 million on Polymarket. Tuesday's vote is the first full test of the platforms' claim to forecast elections, and of the regulators who have pledged to police insider trading on them.
item.content:encoded:
More than $1.4 billion has been traded on prediction markets about the 2026 midterm elections, according to a CNN analysis of the platforms' public data — nearly $1.1 billion of it on Kalshi, the largest United States operator, and more than $340 million on Polymarket across its United States and offshore platforms. ForecastEx, owned by Interactive Brokers, accounts for more than $6.4 million. The figures measure trading volume — the value of contracts changing hands before markets close — not the sum originally wagered.

The structure of the trading matters more than the total. A nonprofit tracker, the Anti-Corruption Data Collective, counted 21,811 individual congressional markets across the platforms by September 30, with only about 16% of them on who wins a race; the majority trade on margins of victory, and more than $20 million had traded on outcomes that can be known in advance, such as candidate withdrawals and endorsements. Kalshi has suspended at least six 2026 candidates for betting on their own races, CNN reported, and federal regulators have pledged to act on insider trading around the midterms.

Tuesday is the settlement date for the cycle's central claim. Kalshi's chief executive, Tarek Mansour, has described the midterms as a test of market-based forecasting, and Polymarket cites a 98% accuracy rate for its election markets one day before an election — a company figure, carried here as the company's claim. Edition 013 reported Kalshi's $1 billion Series G at a $40 billion valuation and its stated share of the prediction market; what Tuesday adds is a public score. If the markets call the close races well, they enter the next cycle as a forecasting source news organizations cite alongside polls. If they miss, the $1.4 billion reads differently — as volume in search of a result.

item.title: Polynesia’s Genomes Hold Drug Clues the Big Databases Missed
item.description: Genomes from more than 1,000 French Polynesians show founder effects at least ten times stronger than Finland’s — concentrating rare variants until their effects on health become measurable.

item.title: OpenAI Will Train on Daybreak Blue Cybersecurity Sessions From November 29, Sessions Previously Excluded From Training
item.description: OpenAI told members of its Trusted Access for Cyber program that session data from Daybreak Blue, its defensive-security tier, will be used for model training from November 29. Those sessions were previously excluded from training even for users who had switched training off. After members objected, the company promised a separate opt-out whose mechanics it has not described.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI will use session data from Daybreak Blue — the defensive tier of its Trusted Access for Cyber program — to train its models starting November 29, The Decoder reported on October 31, from an email the company sent to program members. Daybreak gives approved security researchers access to models for defensive work such as vulnerability triage, secure code review and incident response. Until this change, Daybreak Blue sessions were excluded from training altogether, including for members who had turned off the general 'improve the model for everyone' setting.

The follow-up reporting on November 1 adds a second source: OpenAI's updated public data-controls page now states that content from Daybreak Blue sessions on personal accounts may be used to improve its models even when that setting is off. The company says the training use is intended to strengthen safeguards against cyber misuse, and that interactions flagged during safety reviews may be used for safety purposes. Activity outside Trusted Access sessions continues to follow the user's setting, and inputs from Business, Enterprise, Edu and API services are not used for training by default.

The response from members was immediate. Security researcher Sean Heelan, in a post cited in the coverage, argued the change takes researchers' private work — sessions that can contain vulnerability details, exploit proofs and client system layouts — and predicted it would reduce use of the program. OpenAI then sent a second email promising a separate opt-out for Daybreak sessions. Neither the emails as reported nor the public page describes how that opt-out will work, what its default will be, or whether it applies to past sessions. The date that governs is November 29: unless the separate control has arrived by then, the default changes on that day.

item.title: A Molecular Brake Slows a Spinning Rotor 300,000-Fold
item.description: Researchers in Prague used light to block a molecular rotor’s spin. At very low temperatures, the braked rotor would need about 350 billion years for a single turn — roughly 25 times the age of the universe.

item.title: A Personal Vaccine Cut Melanoma Recurrence or Death Risk by 42% in a Phase 3 Trial
item.description: A vaccine built from each patient’s own tumor, added to immunotherapy after surgery, reduced the risk of death or recurrence by 42% in 1,137 people with advanced melanoma. The result was reported at a European oncology meeting.

item.title: McDonald's Traffic Fell in the Third Quarter, and Its MONOPOLY Relaunch Produced Its Busiest Weeks of 2026
item.description: Visits to McDonald's fell 4.6% year over year in the third quarter, Placer.ai reports. In October, the return of the MONOPOLY game and Halloween Boo Buckets lifted traffic above the year's weekly average for three straight weeks, without passing the same weeks of 2025.
item.content:encoded:
McDonald's third-quarter traffic fell, and its October promotions worked — both facts arrive in the same report, three days before the company reports earnings. Placer.ai's analysis, published Monday, puts visits down 4.6% year over year in the third quarter and same-store visits down 5.1%, with traffic below the prior year in every month from March through September as higher gasoline prices weighed on household budgets.

October reversed the pattern, on promotions rather than price cuts to the core menu. The relaunch of the MONOPOLY game on October 6 and Disney villain-themed Boo Buckets on October 20 produced the chain's busiest weeks of 2026: traffic ran 2.2% above the year's weekly average in the launch week, 5.4% the next, and 7.2% the week after. The visits still did not exceed the same weeks of 2025, when both promotions also ran. McDonald's reports its third quarter before the open on Wednesday, November 4, and has signaled United States comparable sales likely slipped — which makes Wednesday's question specific: whether a game board and a Halloween bucket moved guest counts enough to change the quarter's story.

item.title: Marble Cognition Raised $3.75 Million for Agent Workers That Learn by Watching Employees Work
item.description: The Munich startup, launched today, records how employees use their tools — screenshots, clicks and keystrokes — and converts the record into a structured process map its agents can execute. The $3.75 million pre-seed was led by Heartcore and Seedcamp. Every figure about what the system captures is the company's; no customer is named in the launch coverage.
item.content:encoded:
Marble Cognition, a Munich startup, launched today with a $3.75 million pre-seed round led by Heartcore and Seedcamp, with angel investors including executives from McKinsey and Mistral AI and a board member of Datadog, SiliconANGLE reported. Marble was co-founded by German AI engineers Felix Rösner and Christophe Schmit. Its premise is that enterprise agents are now widely available, and what companies lack is a record of how their own work is actually done.

The product records work at the source. A desktop application observes employees using their tools and processes — taking screenshots and capturing clicks and keystrokes — and transforms that record into a structured process map that AI agents can read and execute, in the company's description, similar to code. The agents Marble calls its workers are then meant to run the mapped processes.

The company's account leaves the load-bearing questions open. No customer is named in the launch coverage, no accuracy or completion figures are published, and the monitoring at the center of the product — continuous screenshots and keystroke capture of employees — raises consent and works-council questions in its home market that the coverage does not address. What the round establishes is narrower: investors are funding the observation layer beneath enterprise agents, on the theory that the scarce input is not the agent but a faithful map of the work. That is the same scarcity GenRobot sells into for physical work, recorded in this edition — one in factories, one in offices.

item.title: A Common Methyl Donor Sped Liver Regeneration in Mice — and in Patients, in One Study
item.description: Researchers traced how a healing liver protects its growth proteins from disposal, then found that giving the methyl donor SAM accelerated regeneration in both mice and patients. Early evidence, one study.

item.title: GenRobot AI Raised $100 Million to Collect the Human Demonstrations Robots Learn From
item.description: The Beijing company sells the recording systems and software that capture people performing tasks — vision, hand and body movement — and turn the recordings into labeled training data for robots. Its $100 million Series A+ round was disclosed on November 2; the company says it closed in the third quarter. SAIC Motor and Baidu are among the investors named in the disclosure.
item.content:encoded:
GenRobot AI, a Beijing company that builds data infrastructure for robot developers, has completed a $100 million Series A+ round, in a financing disclosed on November 2 that the company says closed in the third quarter. GenRobot does not build robots. It builds the equipment and software used to collect human demonstrations — recordings of people carrying out tasks, capturing vision together with hand and body movement — and its Matrix platform synchronizes, cleans and labels those recordings so robot developers can train on them.

The investor list in the disclosure is broad: SAIC Motor, Baidu, Shoucheng Holdings and Galaxy General Robotics among industrial and strategic names, alongside GL Ventures, CITIC Goldstone, CCB International and Huatai Zijin among financial investors. The terms that would show how the company is valued — price, structure, and any customer or revenue figures — are not in the disclosure, which comes from a single trade report of the company's announcement; this paper has not independently verified the round's terms.

The business exists because of where the bottleneck in physical AI currently sits. A language model trains on text that already exists; a robot model trains on demonstrations that someone has to perform, record and label, task by task. Edition 014's Bleu Robotics made the adjacent bet from the software side — fewer demonstrations per task. GenRobot makes it from the supply side: demonstrations as a produced input, sold to every developer who needs them. Which side of that market keeps the value depends on how scarce clean demonstration data remains once the first generation of robots is deployed and generating its own.

item.title: Four AI Companies Will Honor One robots.txt Signal for Opting Out of AI Training
item.description: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic have each said they will honor a single shared signal in a website's robots.txt file that keeps its content out of generative AI training. One rule would replace the separate block each company requires today. Support arrives on different schedules, running into 2027, and the signal is a statement of preference, not a license.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic have each said they will honor one shared signal that lets a website keep its content out of generative AI training, The Verge reported on October 30. The signal lives in robots.txt, the file sites already use to address crawlers. A site adds a group headed by a new policy token, __usage_ai-training, and lists the paths it does not want used for training — the whole site, or everything except, in the draft's own example, a press kit. Today a publisher who wants to refuse training must write and maintain a separate block for each company's crawler.

A draft, not yet a standard

The text is an individual Internet-Draft at the Internet Engineering Task Force, written by Kevin Kelley, a technical lead for standards at Anthropic, and published on October 30. The IETF has not endorsed it; it has no formal standing in the standards process, and it expires on May 3, 2027 unless advanced. The draft is explicit about its limits: it states a preference about how content is used. It does not block crawling, it does not affect search indexing, and it applies to future training — it cannot withdraw content already collected.

Four schedules

Support arrives at four speeds. Anthropic says it has already begun implementing the signal, as a complement to its existing crawler controls rather than a replacement. OpenAI says it aims to implement it in the coming months, and that its existing controls, including the GPTBot block, remain in force meanwhile. Microsoft will honor the new preferences from February 1, 2027, and will stop recognizing the older tags it used for training preferences after March 1, 2027; Microsoft states that the preferences do not establish licensing or payment arrangements. Google aims to support the signal in 2027: John Mueller, its search advocate, wrote that a site which opts out with the shared token and does not mention Google-Extended will be treated as having blocked Google-Extended, the token that governs Gemini training. Meta's communications head, Andy Stone, voiced support for a common signal, The Verge reported, without saying Meta would honor this one.

What changed on October 30 is therefore narrower than the headline version of the story, and more durable. No publisher gained a new legal right, and no crawler changed its behavior that day. What publishers gained is a single line that four competing laboratories have publicly committed to read — which converts a private configuration chore into a public commitment that can be checked, company by company, against the schedules each one published.

item.title: Five Silicon Qubits Now Share a Single Control Wire
item.description: A RIKEN-led team ran five silicon qubits down one shared microwave line and kept their accuracy at the level error correction requires — attacking the wiring bottleneck that keeps quantum processors small.

item.title: The First Known Fruit-Eating Dinosaur Had Chewing Muscles Built Like a Parrot’s
item.description: A small Cretaceous dinosaur, Infernogallus jamesi, had a chewing-muscle arrangement seen today only in fruit-eating parrots — evidence that some dinosaurs ate fruit, and may have carried the seeds that spread flowering plants.

item.title: East Antarctica’s Ice Sheet Stayed Stable in 100,000-Year Simulations Even Above 10 Degrees of Warming
item.description: In coupled climate simulations, the largest ice sheet on Earth held up under extreme warming because warmer air delivered it more snow and more cloud cover — while West Antarctica and Greenland, in the same simulations, lost heavily.

item.title: Colorectal Cancer in Patients Under 50 Is Biologically Different, a 189-Tumor Study Finds
item.description: Tumors from patients diagnosed before 50 carry proportionally more stromal cells and fewer epithelial cells than tumors from older patients, in the largest study of its kind — a possible reason the disease behaves more aggressively in younger people.

item.title: AI-Designed Virus Shells Delivered Genes to Primate Brains 152 Times Better
item.description: Dyno Therapeutics’ engineered capsids reached the brain far more efficiently than the standard AAV9 in non-human primates, and versions built to evade antibodies tested negative against up to 85% of human serum samples. All of it is preclinical.

item.title: Crushed Shells Mixed Into Beach Sand Helped Young Clams Grow in More Acidic Water
item.description: Adding shell fragments to the sand where baby clams burrow changed the water between the grains, lowered its acidity, and produced larger shells — a measured version of a shell-adding practice Indigenous communities have used for generations.

item.title: Pines Planted Far From Home Grow Up to Four Times Faster, and Handle Drought Better
item.description: Across 192 sites on four continents, conifers planted in the Southern Hemisphere outgrew the same species at home — and stored more sugars and starches, a reserve that appears to carry them through dry spells.

item.title: Cells Can Now Record What They Were Doing Days Ago
item.description: Engineered organelles archive a cell’s own RNA as it works — so days later, researchers can read back which genes were active, including in the rare cancer cells that survive chemotherapy and seed relapse.

item.title: A Structure Called the Cat’s Tail Records a Pluto-Scale Collision 63 Light-Years Away
item.description: Hubble has imaged the Cat’s Tail in visible light for the first time: a dark stream about 1,000 times the Earth–Sun distance across, inside a young star’s debris disk — evidence of a collision between bodies the size of Pluto.

item.title: Starving Ants Protect Their Brains’ Energy First, Like Humans Do
item.description: When food runs short, ants keep supplying their brains at a rate comparable to the share humans protect — even though a colony is supposed to put the group ahead of any individual.

item.title: A 237-Million-Year-Old Amphibian Appears to Have Lived Its Whole Life in the Ocean
item.description: No amphibian lives in the sea today. Chemical signatures in two armored fossils found in China match seawater, not the local rock — evidence of a marine amphibian 30 kilometers from the nearest possible island.

item.title: A Debut Winner in New York: Almgren Takes the Marathon in 2:06:01, Chepkirui the Women's Race
item.description: Andreas Almgren won the New York City Marathon in 2:06:01 in the first marathon of his career, and Sheila Chepkirui won the women's race in 2:24:36, six seconds ahead of American Jessica McClain. Nearly 60,000 runners contested the 50th running of the five-borough course.
item.content:encoded:
Andreas Almgren of Sweden won the TCS New York City Marathon on Sunday in 2:06:01 — in the first marathon of his career. Almgren, the world half-marathon champion, broke away from a lead group that had stayed together through 35 kilometers and finished 13 seconds ahead of Italy's Yemaneberhan Crippa. Kamohelo Mofolo of Lesotho was third in 2:06:26 on his 21st birthday, one second ahead of defending champion Benson Kipruto. Almgren is the first Swede to win the race, and the first man to win it on debut since 2010.

The women's race was decided in the final meters. Sheila Chepkirui of Kenya won her second New York title in 2:24:36, pulling clear of defending champion Hellen Obiri late. Jessica McClain of the United States passed Obiri in the last 30 meters to finish second in 2:24:42 — the first American woman on the New York podium since Shalane Flanagan in 2018. Nearly 60,000 runners took part in the 50th running of the five-borough course, a race-day record, on a course run with its first material change in more than a decade.

item.title: A Preference Is Not a License
item.description: Four competing laboratories agreeing to read the same opt-out line is a real change: consent for training data is moving from a set of separate crawler blocks, maintained company by company, to a shared signal any site can write once. The limits are in the fine print the companies themselves published.
item.content:encoded: Four competing laboratories agreeing to read the same opt-out line is a real change: consent for training data is moving from a set of separate crawler blocks, maintained company by company, to a shared signal any site can write once. The limits are in the fine print the companies themselves published. The signal is voluntary. It covers future training only, it arrives on schedules that run into 2027, and Microsoft states plainly that it establishes no licensing or payment arrangement. A publisher who writes the line today has recorded a preference. Whether that preference becomes a right depends on enforcement that does not yet exist.

item.title: Malware Now Hands Stolen Data to an AI Model and Asks What the Victim Is Worth
item.description: Cisco Talos documented a Windows infostealer that, after taking passwords, cookies and payment cards, sends the haul to a commercial AI model with instructions to rank the victim's most valuable assets. If the first model refuses, the malware tries a second, then a third. Talos reports no evidence the malware has been used in real attacks.
item.content:encoded:
Cisco Talos published its analysis of a Windows infostealer it calls VOLTA on October 31. The theft side is conventional and thorough: browser credentials, cookies and saved payment cards from Chromium browsers, Firefox and Thunderbird; session tokens for Discord, Telegram, Steam and Roblox; Microsoft OAuth tokens; cryptocurrency wallet material; SSH and cloud configuration files; Wi-Fi profiles and screenshots. Talos says the malware then uses stolen access to enrich the haul, searching a victim's email for purchase receipts and pulling delivery histories.

The new part comes after the theft. VOLTA assembles the collected material into a structured bundle and, when it has an API key, sends it through OpenRouter to a commercial AI model. Its prompt tells the model to act as a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment, with sections headed 'WHAT THEY'RE WORTH' — valuables ranked by how easily they can be turned into money — and 'THEIR OPSEC,' an assessment of the victim's security habits. The default model is Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6. The malware scans each reply for refusal phrases such as 'I can't,' and on a refusal falls back to Moonshot's Kimi K2 and then to Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash. The output is saved as a file named AI_Analysis.txt and exfiltrated with the rest.

Talos is explicit about the limits of the finding. The researchers, led by Ryan Fetterman, found VOLTA through CAIRN, a toolkit Talos open-sourced on September 22 for hunting malware with built-in AI. They have not reported whether any of the three models complied or refused in testing, and they have not tracked the malware in use in real attacks; the sample was first seen on October 11. Without a configured API key, the AI stage is skipped and VOLTA works as an ordinary stealer. The significance of the sample is the division of labor it assumes: the commodity part of an intrusion is no longer reading what was stolen, because a rented model will read it, rank it and write the summary.

item.title: Alibaba's Qwen Will Power Apple Intelligence in China, With Testing From November 4
item.description: Apple and Alibaba announced on Saturday that Qwen will supply the model behind Siri, Writing Tools and Visual Intelligence for iPhone users in China. Testing starts November 4 in the developer beta; the public release is planned for December. The rebuilt Siri assistant is not part of the package.
item.content:encoded:
Apple Intelligence is coming to iPhones in mainland China on a Chinese model. Apple announced on its China newsroom on Saturday that testing begins November 4 in the latest iOS developer beta, with a public release planned for December in iOS 27.3. Alibaba confirmed the partnership the same day: its Qwen models will be integrated into Siri, Writing Tools and Visual Intelligence, covering text and image understanding and content generation. Alibaba's chief executive, Eddie Wu, said Qwen would be deeply integrated across Apple's ecosystem.

The arrangement reflects the regulatory structure of the market. Generative AI services in China require local approval, and reporting on the announcement notes that China's cyberspace regulator registered Apple's on-device generative AI service in July. In China, Qwen stands in the position ChatGPT occupies elsewhere in Apple Intelligence: for certain requests, Siri can pass a question to Qwen and draw on its knowledge, and a Compose option in Writing Tools lets it draft original text. The integration is opt-in — users choose whether to enable it and what to share — and Alibaba says requests sent through Apple Intelligence, and the responses generated, will not be used to train its models.

What Chinese users are getting is the first generation of the product, two years after its United States launch. Apple's announcement states that the December release does not include Siri AI or the other next-generation Apple Intelligence features announced at its 2026 developers conference — the rebuilt assistant now rolling out elsewhere is not in this package. Eligibility is narrow: an Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone bought in China, or a device whose location and Apple Account region are both set to China, with support for other Apple platforms to follow after further approvals. The first outside check on the arrangement arrives quickly: developers can test Qwen's behavior inside Siri and Writing Tools from Tuesday's beta.

item.title: Pope Leo XIV Asked States to Ban Lethal Autonomous Weapons at November Talks in Geneva
item.description: Addressing AI researchers at the Vatican on Friday, Pope Leo XIV said decisions over human life and the use of force must remain under human control, rejected legal personhood for AI systems, and urged states meeting in Geneva in November toward a prohibition of lethal autonomous weapons.
item.content:encoded:
Pope Leo XIV used an address to AI researchers at the Vatican on Friday, October 30, to ask states meeting in Geneva in November to take concrete steps toward prohibiting lethal autonomous weapons. Decisions affecting human life, freedom and the use of force, he said, must always remain subject to effective, informed and responsible human control, and artificial intelligence must be 'disarmed.' The meeting — 'The Future of AI: A Dialogue between the Vatican and the Scientific World' — was organized by the Pontifical Academy for Life and the Future of Life Institute.

The address restated the position of his May encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas, in five considerations, and drew a line his predecessor also drew: Pope Francis told the G7 in 2024 that no machine should ever choose to take a human life. Leo rejected proposals to grant AI systems legal personhood — 'Machines are instruments, not people' — arguing that responsibility for a system's actions rests with its human creators and operators, and called for shared international standards, independent oversight and clear mechanisms of accountability. The remarks are a moral appeal to negotiators, not law; no state has committed to the ban ahead of the Geneva talks. In a separate note of the same week, the Holy See Press Office confirmed that the Pope, who was born in Chicago, has already mailed his ballot for Tuesday's United States midterm elections.

item.title: Permission Is Now a Line Item
item.description: A judge held that the turbines powering xAI's Colossus site are not exempt from air permits, so whether they were ever permitted will be argued in full. The ruling decides no liability — and that is the point: permission has moved from a filing made before construction to a legal exposure carried during operation.
item.content:encoded: A data center used to need land, power and capital. The ruling in Mississippi adds a fourth requirement in a form builders cannot schedule around: a judge held that the turbines powering xAI's Colossus site are not exempt from air permits, so the question of whether they were ever permitted will be argued in full. The ruling decides no liability, and that is the point. Permission has moved from a filing made before construction to a legal exposure carried during operation, at a cost counted in time and in public. October's scarcest input was a grid connection. November's may be consent.

item.title: The New York City Marathon Runs Its 50th Five-Borough Race Today
item.description: The TCS New York City Marathon runs today on the 50th anniversary of its five-borough course, with both defending champions — Benson Kipruto, who won last year by three hundredths of a second, and Hellen Obiri, the women's course-record holder — and an extra hour in the morning, returned by the overnight clock change.
item.content:encoded:
The TCS New York City Marathon runs today, Sunday, November 1, on the 50th anniversary of the race's five-borough course. The professional women start at 8:35 a.m. Eastern and the professional men at 9:05 a.m., on a morning made longer by the calendar: clocks went back one hour at 2 a.m., so the race's early waves start on the extra hour the fall change returns.

Both defending champions are back. Benson Kipruto of Kenya won the men's race last year by three hundredths of a second over Alexander Mutiso — the closest finish in the race's history — and Hellen Obiri returns after setting the women's course record of 2:19:51 last November. Obiri's challengers include Sheila Chepkirui, the 2024 champion, and Edna Kiplagat, who won in 2010. Two expected contenders are absent: Olympic champion Sifan Hassan withdrew after illness disrupted her preparation, and American Fiona O'Keeffe is out with an injury. The American men's race pairs Conner Mantz, the national record holder at 2:04:43, against Zouhair Talbi, whose 2:03:45 in Boston in April is the fastest marathon run by an American, on a course not eligible for records.

item.title: A Federal Judge Let the Lawsuit Over xAI's Data Center Turbines Proceed
item.description: A federal judge denied xAI's request to dismiss a Clean Air Act lawsuit over the gas turbines powering its Colossus data center outside Memphis. The court rejected the company's argument that the turbines are mobile equipment exempt from air permits. The ruling decides no liability; it means the permit question will now be heard in full.
item.content:encoded:
A federal judge has denied xAI's motion to dismiss a Clean Air Act lawsuit over the gas turbines powering its Colossus data center outside Memphis, TechCrunch reported on Saturday. Judge Debra M. Brown of the US District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi ruled that the plaintiffs have standing under the Clean Air Act, that the turbines are not 'mobile sources' under Mississippi's state implementation plan, and that the Act's citizen-suit provision does not violate the Constitution. The ruling, released on Friday, October 30, allows the case to proceed. It does not decide whether xAI violated the Act.

What the suit alleges

The NAACP and the Mississippi State Conference of the NAACP filed the case on April 14, 2026, represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center. The center says xAI 'installed and operated at least 35 combustion turbines and other sources of air pollution at the Colossus site without ever obtaining the necessary preconstruction or operating air permits.' The complaint in the Mississippi case, as summarized in Saturday's coverage, alleges that X.AI Corp. and MZX Tech LLC installed and operated 27 gas turbines in Southaven, Mississippi, from August to December 2025 without an air permit, and that the turbines powered AI data centers in the Memphis area and emitted smog-forming pollutants and particulate matter. xAI's defense was procedural: the turbines are mobile, and therefore exempt; the plaintiffs lack standing; and citizen suits of this kind are unconstitutional. The court rejected each argument at this stage.

The second ruling in a month

This is the second dismissal attempt the case has survived in October. On October 19, the same court allowed the federal government to intervene in the case while denying its request to end it. Abre' Connor, the NAACP's director of environmental and climate justice, described Saturday's outcome as 'another important victory in our effort to hold xAI accountable.' xAI is now owned by SpaceX; the company has not, in the reporting, answered the underlying allegation — whether the permits were required and were not obtained.

The case lands inside a thread this paper has followed since its first edition: the buildout's binding constraint is power, and power is obtained in public. Edition 001's lead was a data center abandoned for want of a grid connection; Edition 005 recorded moratoria, grid queues and local opposition delaying projects. The Colossus ruling is the courtroom version of the same constraint. A builder can install turbines faster than a grid connection can be approved; what Saturday's ruling establishes is that the speed does not settle the permission, and that the permission question can be litigated while the machines run.

item.title: Five Silicon Qubits Now Share a Single Control Wire
item.description: A RIKEN-led team ran five silicon qubits down one shared microwave line and kept their accuracy at the level error correction requires — attacking the wiring bottleneck that keeps quantum processors small.

item.title: The First Known Fruit-Eating Dinosaur Had Chewing Muscles Built Like a Parrot’s
item.description: A small Cretaceous dinosaur, Infernogallus jamesi, had a chewing-muscle arrangement seen today only in fruit-eating parrots — evidence that some dinosaurs ate fruit, and may have carried the seeds that spread flowering plants.

item.title: East Antarctica’s Ice Sheet Stayed Stable in 100,000-Year Simulations Even Above 10 Degrees of Warming
item.description: In coupled climate simulations, the largest ice sheet on Earth held up under extreme warming because warmer air delivered it more snow and more cloud cover — while West Antarctica and Greenland, in the same simulations, lost heavily.

item.title: Colorectal Cancer in Patients Under 50 Is Biologically Different, a 189-Tumor Study Finds
item.description: Tumors from patients diagnosed before 50 carry proportionally more stromal cells and fewer epithelial cells than tumors from older patients, in the largest study of its kind — a possible reason the disease behaves more aggressively in younger people.

item.title: AI-Designed Virus Shells Delivered Genes to Primate Brains 152 Times Better
item.description: Dyno Therapeutics’ engineered capsids reached the brain far more efficiently than the standard AAV9 in non-human primates, and versions built to evade antibodies tested negative against up to 85% of human serum samples. All of it is preclinical.

item.title: Crushed Shells Mixed Into Beach Sand Helped Young Clams Grow in More Acidic Water
item.description: Adding shell fragments to the sand where baby clams burrow changed the water between the grains, lowered its acidity, and produced larger shells — a measured version of a shell-adding practice Indigenous communities have used for generations.
